fact: The USGA's 2018 recommendations for building putting greens say the subgrade's slope should follow the general slope of the finished green, the collar belongs inside the green's cavity, fill goes in 6-inch lifts compacted to at least 90 percent of standard Proctor density, the subgrade is shaped with no water-collecting depressions, and the gravel layer follows the finished grade within 1 inch.
quote: The slope of the subgrade should conform to the general slope of the finished grade. … Include the collar area as part of the putting green cavity. If fill soil is used to construct the putting green subgrade, the soil should be placed in 6-inch lifts and compacted to at least 90 percent of minimum standard Proctor density ASTM D698. The subgrade should be shaped to avoid any water-collecting depressions and thoroughly compacted to prevent settling. … [the gravel layer] shall conform to the proposed finished grade, plus or minus 1 inch.
source_label: USGA Recommendations for a Method of Putting Green Construction, 2018 Revision, Steps 2 and 4 (Michigan State University Turfgrass Information Center copy)
notes: Read the full 2018 document (PDF text) at the MSU Turfgrass Information Center, which archives USGA publications; usga.org's construction page returns 403 to automated fetches. Written for natural-grass greens; the page applies only the shaping and compaction principles to a synthetic green's base.

fact: The USGA's 2018 putting green recommendations say that where the subsoil is unstable, as with expanding clays, the builder should consult geotechnical engineers familiar with local soils about stabilizing it.
quote: If the subsoil is unstable – as may be the case with expanding clays, sand or highly organic soils – consult geotechnical engineers familiar with local soils for soil-stabilization recommendations.
source_label: USGA Recommendations for a Method of Putting Green Construction, 2018 Revision, Step 2 (Michigan State University Turfgrass Information Center copy)

fact: The USGA's 2018 recommendations run a putting green's main drain pipes along the lines of maximum fall and add lateral drains in any water-collecting depressions.
quote: The pattern of drainage pipes should be designed so that the main drains are placed along the lines of maximum fall. … Laterals should also be placed in water-collecting depressions if they exist.
source_label: USGA Recommendations for a Method of Putting Green Construction, 2018 Revision, Step 3 (Michigan State University Turfgrass Information Center copy)

fact: A USGA Green Section agronomist wrote in 1982 that a green's contours should let surface water leave in at least two, and preferably three or four, directions, with no more than 60% of the runoff going one way and the water directed away from the normal line of play.
quote: Putting surfaces and collars should be designed so that surface water is drained away rapidly and efficiently. Contouring of the green should provide a minimum of two, and preferably, three or four directions in which surface water can flow. No more than 60% of the surface run-off should be drained in a single direction. Water should be directed away from the normal line of play, yet all too often greens are designed with a single surface drainage pattern which directs the water to the approach area of the front of the green.
source_label: Brian Silva (USGA Green Section agronomist), Proper Green Construction Solves Problems Later, Weeds Trees & Turf, March 1982, pp. 48 and 50 (Michigan State University Turfgrass Information Center scan)
notes: The scan's OCR reads the figure as "6 0 %"; the printed page reads 60%. The sentence continues on p. 50.

fact: The same 1982 article warns that in cold climates a green that drains back to front can ice over, because snow melting at the back during a warm winter day runs the length of the green and refreezes as the late afternoon cools, and says low spots, pockets and water channeled over narrow parts of the collar should be avoided.
quote: In cold climates, these back-to-front drainage greens are susceptible to ice cover formation as snow cover melts at the rear of the green during the warm part of a winter day. The water then has to travel the length of the green in leaving the putting surface and often refreezes as temperatures drop in the late afternoon and early evening. Additionally, low spots and pockets should be avoided as should channeling of the water over restricted portions of the green collar.
source_label: Brian Silva (USGA Green Section agronomist), Proper Green Construction Solves Problems Later, Weeds Trees & Turf, March 1982, p. 50 (Michigan State University Turfgrass Information Center scan)

fact: ASGCA past president John LaFoy writes that green contours are as individual as fingerprints but every successful green must be playable, and describes running mounds from the green's perimeter onto the putting surface to create contour without using up the area where cups can go, with each cupping area giving a relatively easy putt within fifteen or twenty feet.
quote: Green contouring is about as individual as fingerprints. However, all successful greens must have one thing in common. They must be playable. … While some skilled designers prefer to put most of their movement within the putting surface proper, others like to incorporate the movement on the perimeter of the surfaces and run it onto the surfaces. An example of this would be carefully placing mounds around the perimeter of the green and tailing the mounds onto the putting surface. By doing this, you create some very interesting contours without using up too much of the cuppable area within the putting surface. … Balls stopping within the appropriate segment should offer a relatively easy putt within fifteen or twenty feet. Balls stopping on the edge of the green or in a different segment of the putting surface may require a double break or putting over a mound.
source_label: John LaFoy (ASGCA past president), Green Design, American Society of Golf Course Architects
notes: The article writes the distances as words (fifteen or twenty feet); the page may give them as 15 to 20 feet. Undated on the ASGCA site.

fact: LaFoy writes that older multi-level greens often lose a third to a half of their cuppable area to the slope between levels, and that the slope between levels should be over-exaggerated in the first grading because it mellows as the layers are built up over it.
quote: The secret to building a functional multi-level green is in the transition between the platforms. Many of the older multi-level greens use way too much of the putting surface in the transition between levels. It is not unusual to see as much as a third or half of a green un-cuppable due to the transition slope. It is critical, during the initial grading of a multi-level green, to over exaggerate the slope between the two levels. It is also critical that the slope between the levels be flat and not convex or humped. As the green is built up with the various rock and top mix layers, the slope begins to mellow.
source_label: John LaFoy (ASGCA past president), Green Design, American Society of Golf Course Architects

fact: LaFoy defines a green complex as the putting surface plus greenside bunkers, grass hollows, slopes and shoulders, and says many architects look at a green site from where the approach shot lands to picture the new green, which should fit the natural flow of the ground.
quote: The word “green complex” is used, because it includes the putting surface, greenside bunkers and grass hollows, and slopes and shoulders. … Every architect probably has a different way of starting their preliminary design, but many find it useful to view the green complexes from the landing area to visualize what the new green will look like. Of course, with the base map in hand, showing the topography of the existing green complex, the proposed green should fit into the natural flow of the ground.
source_label: John LaFoy (ASGCA past president), Green Design, American Society of Golf Course Architects

fact: In a 2018 USGA article, superintendents describe spreading hole locations evenly between left, right, middle, front and back, keeping them at least five paces (about 15 feet) from a green's edges though no rule requires it, and choosing spots where puddling is least likely in wet weather.
quote: We try to create a fairly equal distribution of hole locations between left, right, middle, front and back. … We keep hole locations a minimum of five paces – approximately 15 feet – from the edges of a green. Many golfers are not aware that while there are rules about the size of the hole and the depth of the liner, there is no rule about how far from the edge of a putting green the hole must be located. … During wet periods, or when wet weather is forecast, we ask our course setters to choose hole locations where puddling is least likely.
source_label: Larry Gilhuly (USGA agronomist), Hole Location, Location, Location, USGA Fore the Golfer, Aug. 17, 2018
notes: usga.org returns 403 to curl and WebFetch; read in a browser on 2026-09-26. The quoted lines are superintendents' answers the USGA article prints.

fact: A 2002 USGA Green Section Record article says every collar gives the golfer an intermediate surface between the green and the rough, so a shot that barely misses or rolls through the green is not severely penalized, that a new green's collar should be built as part of the green, and that there is no standard collar width.
quote: Although the width and height of cut vary among golf courses, all collars serve the important role of providing the golfer an intermediate surface between the putting green and surrounding rough. The collar helps prevent the player from being severely penalized for shots that barely miss or roll through the putting green. … When building new putting greens, the collar should be built as part of the green … Although there is no standard for collar width, a width that enables mowing with a single pass saves time.
source_label: Matt Nelson, Collar ID, USGA Green Section Record, July-August 2002, p. 9 (Michigan State University archive)
notes: The same article says collars can be set to a 22- or 26-inch width for one pass of a walk mower.

fact: A 2022 USGA Green Section Record article says a collar's purpose is a buffer between the green and the primary rough, makes sense where the green would otherwise meet tall rough, and adds little where an intermediate cut around 1 inch high already surrounds the green.
quote: The purpose of a collar is to provide a buffer between the putting green and primary rough surrounding the green. If the collar transitions directly to rough that is quite tall, one can make a strong argument that a collar is sensible. However, many courses have an intermediate rough cut maintained around 1 inch in height that already provides a buffer between the green and primary rough.
source_label: Darin Bevard, Strategies to Prevent Putting Green Collar Decline, USGA Green Section Record, Vol. 60, Issue 06 (April 1, 2022)
notes: usga.org returns 403 to automated fetches; read in a browser on 2026-09-26.

fact: A 2020 USGA Green Section Record article says wind erosion can cost a bunker significant sand, that bunker liners cannot stop contamination carried by wind or surface water, and that grading around bunkers should keep surface water and its debris out.
quote: Wind erosion can result in significant sand loss from bunkers, which increases costs due to sand replacement and the labor necessary to install the sand. … While bunker liners help reduce contamination from the subsoil, they cannot prevent contamination carried by wind or surface water. … Grading around bunkers should discourage surface water, and the debris it carries, from entering bunkers.
source_label: Brian Whitlark, A Guide To Selecting the Right Bunker Sand for Your Course, USGA Green Section Record, Vol. 58, Issue 11 (June 5, 2020)
notes: usga.org returns 403 to automated fetches; read in a browser on 2026-09-26.

fact: The same article reports bunker sand infiltration falling from 22.8 to 7.5 inches per hour within two to three years as wind-blown dust, clippings, leaves, algae and soil clog it, and says 4 to 6 inches of sand on a bunker floor has historically worked.
quote: in my experience testing bunker sands on golf courses, I’ve seen that infiltration rates often decrease significantly – e.g., from 22.8 to only 7.5 inches per hour – in just two to three years! Silt and clay from wind-blown dust, organic debris from clippings, leaves from trees or shrubs, algae growth and soil contamination all can decrease infiltration rates. … Historically, 4-6 inches of sand depth on the bunker floors has yielded good results
source_label: Brian Whitlark, A Guide To Selecting the Right Bunker Sand for Your Course, USGA Green Section Record, Vol. 58, Issue 11 (June 5, 2020)
notes: usga.org returns 403 to automated fetches; read in a browser on 2026-09-26.

fact: Tour Greens, a synthetic putting green builder, says some contours and undulations go into a green while the soil is compacted and more are built in as its two-layer base of crushed stone and stone dust is compacted.
quote: Once the land has been cleared, workers prepare the soil base with a compacting machine. Some contours and undulations are built into the green at this time. … Once the soil layer is compacted and the Geotextile is installed, we add a two-layer base of compacted crushed stone and stone dust. During this process, we can build in additional shapes and contours to the green.

fact: Tour Greens says tee boxes and other features are usually built at the same time as the green, and that a backyard green is often installed as part of a major landscaping project.
quote: Of course, if you have tee boxes or other features in your design, we are probably working on these at the same time that we are installing the green. Shown here is a hitting area with multiple tee boxes and a sand trap. … It is not uncommon that the installation of a backyard golf green is combined with a major landscaping project.

fact: Tour Greens starts a residential design by asking whether the green is for putting and chipping only or longer shots, how much space there is for the green and any tee boxes or mats, whether the owner wants contours and extra cuts of fringe or rough turf, how fast it should roll, and whether to add sand bunkers, grass bunkers, mounding, retaining walls or hardscape.
quote: Will this green be used for putting and chipping only or for longer shots? How much space is available for the green and potential tee boxes or chipping/hitting mats? Are there specific characteristics that you desire for your putting green? Contours and undulations? Additional cuts of turf to simulate shots from fringe or rough? How fast do you want the green to roll? Are you interested in additional landscaping or practice elements (sand bunkers, grass bunkers, mounding, retaining walls, hardscape additions, etc.)
source_label: Tour Greens, Residential Putting Green Design

fact: Greenline Artificial Grass's putting green installation guide sets the rough grade for drainage first, allows 1 to 2 feet of fringe turf around the green's outline, sculpts levels and breaks into the base, and runs the turf's grain in one direction.
quote: Establish rough grade for drainage (slope/crown) … Use marking paint to draw preliminary design of putting green shape. Allow for 1’-2’ of surrounding fringe turf for perimeter outline. … Sculpt or create varying levels and or breaks for challenging design. … Always run grain of turf in the same direction.
source_label: Greenline Artificial Grass, Synthetic Turf Putting Green Installation Guide (PDF)
